videos.caption: Trump says immigration enforcement may have gone too far, but is he changing his position or testing whether Republicans would support immigration reform? After suggesting his administration's immigration crackdown may have been too aggressive, President Trump quickly defended his tough enforcement policies. But what if these seemingly conflicting statements are part of a larger political strategy? Immigration was a major issue in the 2026 midterm elections, and the results have raised questions about whether Republicans may need to reconsider their approach. One possibility is that Trump is testing the reaction of his conservative base before considering a bipartisan immigration deal. He may recognize the political pressure to address immigration while remaining cautious about losing support from his most loyal voters. But here's where things get interesting: Congress doesn't necessarily need Trump's approval to pass immigration reform. If enough Republicans join Democrats in supporting legislation, Congress could potentially override a presidential veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. That raises an important question about the future of immigration policy. Could moderate Republicans and Democrats find enough common ground to pass meaningful immigration reform, even without the president's support? The possibility of bipartisan cooperation has existed before. Whether lawmakers are willing to pursue it again remains to be seen.
